body.heading: The famous four
paragraphs: Ask a poet for a word that rhymes with orange and watch them smile ruefully. Orange has no perfect rhyme in English — nor do silver, purple or month. They are common, useful words that sit in the language like islands, with no rhyming neighbour to visit.

A perfect rhyme must match from the stressed vowel to the end: cat and hat, moonlight and starlight. Near misses like “door hinge” for orange are called slant rhymes, and songwriters use them happily — but strictly speaking, the island stays unvisited.

body.heading: Why these words are stranded
paragraphs: Rhymes depend on how many words share a sound pattern. Endings like -urple and -onth are rare in English, so purple and month have almost no company. The language simply never built a neighbourhood around their sounds.

Determined rhymers have tried to help. A sporange is a real (if obscure) botanical word for a spore case, sometimes offered as orange's rhyme — but it is pronounced slightly differently, and purists shake their heads. The argument itself has become part of the fun.

body.heading: Try it: rhyme or island?
paragraphs: Deal out word cards — window, elbow, wolf, ninth, music, penguin, chaos, rhythm — and sort them into “has a rhyme” and “island” piles. (Window has window's friends like... check carefully: elbow pairs with nothing perfect either; it is sneakier than it looks.)
Then write a four-line poem that smuggles one island word into the last line, where no rhyme is owed. Poets have used that escape hatch for centuries — now it is yours.

takeaway: Orange and silver are islands in the dictionary: no rhyme reaches them, and poets love them all the more for it.
